title: YouTube 11: What Happens When Your Bank Collapses?

lines.text: On March ninth, twenty twenty-three, customers pulled forty-two billion dollars out of one single bank. In one day.

title: $42 BILLION
OUT OF ONE BANK – IN ONE DAY

lines.text: The next morning, another hundred billion was lined up to leave. And by lunchtime, the bank was gone.
So what actually happens to your money when your bank collapses? And could it happen to your bank, too?
To understand that, you first need to know one slightly uncomfortable secret about banks.
When you put a thousand dollars into your account, the bank doesn't just keep it in a vault.
It lends most of it out to people buying homes and cars, or invests it in things like government bonds.
In the US, banks don't even have to keep a minimum share in reserve anymore. Since March twenty twenty, that requirement is zero percent.
And that works perfectly well, as long as not everyone wants their money back on the same day.
When they do, it's called a bank run. And history shows how brutal that can get.
Between nineteen thirty and nineteen thirty-three, around nine thousand American banks shut their doors.
Millions of families lost their savings, because back then, nothing protected their deposits.
And it's not just history. In two thousand seven, people lined up outside Northern Rock in Britain. It was the first bank run in the UK since Victorian times.
So in nineteen thirty-three, the US created the FDIC. Its deposit insurance started on January first, nineteen thirty-four.
Today, it covers two hundred fifty thousand dollars per person, per bank, per account type.
And since nineteen thirty-four, no depositor has lost a single penny of insured money.
Other countries do the same. The European Union protects one hundred thousand euros, and the UK, one hundred twenty thousand pounds.
So why did Silicon Valley Bank still turn into a disaster?
Its customers were mostly startups and tech companies, with accounts far above the limit. About eighty-six percent of its deposits were not insured.
The bank had put a huge part of that money into long-term bonds. Then interest rates shot up, and those bonds lost value.
Selling them now would mean locking in those losses. Keeping them meant the bank had less cash on hand than it looked.
On March eighth, the bank admitted that it had sold bonds at a one point eight billion dollar loss, and that it needed to raise new money.
Founders warned each other in group chats and on social media. Within hours, everyone tried to get out at once.
In just two days, customers tried to pull out about eighty-one percent of all deposits. And this time, nobody had to stand in line. They just tapped a button.
On March tenth, regulators shut it down. It was the third-largest bank failure in American history.
And suddenly, real companies had their cash stuck inside. The streaming company Roku had about four hundred eighty-seven million dollars there. That was a quarter of all its cash.
The crypto company Circle had three point three billion dollars stuck. Its digital dollar, which is supposed to be worth exactly one dollar, fell below eighty-seven cents.
Then came the weekend that saved everyone.
On March twelfth, the government decided that all depositors would get their money back, even above the limit. And it was paid for with a special fee on other banks.
But the fear kept spreading. Signature Bank in New York fell that same weekend, and in May, First Republic in San Francisco collapsed too.
With two hundred twenty-nine billion dollars in assets, First Republic became the second-largest bank failure ever in the US.
And then, the fear jumped across the Atlantic.
Credit Suisse, a hundred sixty-seven year old Swiss bank, had to be rescued. On March nineteenth, its rival UBS bought it for just three billion Swiss francs.
And some investors lost everything. Sixteen billion francs in special bonds were written down to zero.
So, what happens to your money if your bank fails?
If you're under the limit, usually almost nothing. Most of the time, a healthy bank takes over your account, and you can use your money right away.
If no bank steps in, the FDIC sends you a check, and payments usually begin within a few days.
Only the money above the limit is at risk. You become a creditor of the failed bank, and you might get some of it back, or not.
So here's what you can do. First, keep your savings under the limit at each bank. If you have more, spread it across several banks.
Second, make sure your bank is actually insured. Some apps look like banks, but they aren't banks themselves.
And third, don't panic. Bank runs are what kill banks. Your insured money is safe, even when the headlines look scary.
Would you have pulled your money out of Silicon Valley Bank? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe for more money explained simply.
